To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

self-discipline outdoes intelligence in predicting academic performance and that self-discipline is a better predictor of academic performance than are measures of family socioeconomic status and parental education, even after controlling for intelligence.
self-discipline is the best predictor of academic achievement and that self-discipline outperforms all other predictors, including intelligence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a self-discipline construct, the measurement of self-discipline in adolescents, and the relations between self-discipline and other variables of interest.
the development of self-regulatory processes, particularly those that are related to self-discipline and self-control.
the question of why students fall short of their intellectual promise.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-discipline is a better predictor than IQ of the school performance of adolescents.
self-discipline is the most powerful factor in the academic success of students.
self-discipline is the most important predictor of success in life.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
self-discipline is the glue that holds together all of the other factors that contribute to school and life success.
self-discipline is the glue that binds together all of the other good things that parents and educators try to instill in children.

The main takeaway from our work is that
self-discipline is a better predictor of academic success than is IQ.
self-control is more important than IQ in determining academic performance, and self-control is more malleable than IQ.
self-discipline, which is a teachable skill, is a much better predictor of success in school, in life, and in business than IQ.
